cards.why: Direct sums ask whether communicating about many tasks together can save a substantial fraction of the single-task cost. They connect communication lower bounds with interactive compression and the distinction between information revealed and bits transmitted. The exact error and task conventions determine which savings are possible.

cards.definitions:
In a two-party communication task, Alice knows \(x\), Bob knows \(y\), and they exchange bits to produce a valid output. A function has one correct output for each allowed pair; a relation can permit several. A total function is defined on every pair in the product of the two finite input sets. A partial function or relation can impose an input promise.

For a task \(f\), its \(k\)-fold direct sum \(f^{k}\) gives Alice \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\) and Bob \(y_{1},\ldots,y_{k}\), and requires an output for every corresponding pair. It does not ask only for the parity or disjunction of the outputs. In a worst-case formulation the input tuples are arbitrary; calling the copies independent does not provide a sampling distribution.

One common convention writes \(R_{\varepsilon}(f)\) for the minimum worst-case number of communicated bits of a public-coin randomized interactive protocol that errs with probability at most \(\varepsilon\) on each allowed input pair. The parties have unbounded local computation, shared random bits, and may also use private random bits. A designated party outputs the answer; messages and any communicated output bits count, but local computation does not.

Under the global-error convention, \(R_{\varepsilon}(f^{k})\) requires the entire tuple of \(k\) answers to be valid with probability at least \(1-\varepsilon\). Requiring each coordinate separately to be correct with that probability is a weaker condition. An expected-communication measure averages protocol length over random coins for each input, while worst-case communication bounds every transcript. A distributional measure instead fixes an input distribution and permits average error under it.

A strong version would seek a universal \(c>0\) such that
\[R_{1/3}(f^{k})\geq c\,k\,R_{1/3}(f)\]
for every task in a specified class and every integer \(k\geq1\). Allowing logarithmic losses, changing the single-copy error, taking a limit for a fixed task, or making the constant depend on the task produces different assertions. This displayed formula illustrates a precise version; the source paragraph does not establish that it is the exact intended claim for all relations or for total functions.

These distinctions must be chosen together. The card does not replace randomized communication by nondeterministic communication or by a parity decision-tree model, and does not turn a theorem about information revealed into a theorem about bits transmitted without its required assumptions.
cards.answer_criterion: First fix the task class, randomness, input and communication-cost conventions, errors and allowed loss in the lower bound. A solution must then prove the resulting universally quantified direct-sum assertion or refute it with a family whose joint complexity violates that bound. An amortized theorem for one error convention or a counterexample using relations does not automatically settle a total-function, global-error version.

context_blocks.text: The source contrasts near-perfect nondeterministic direct sums with failures in a deterministic setting and an open randomized setting. It is a brief motivation for studying composition, not a formal statement of all the conventions needed for this benchmark.

context_blocks.title: Per-coordinate amortization is already characterized
context_blocks.text: Braverman and Rao’s report characterizes amortized distributional communication by internal information cost when error is bounded separately on each coordinate. Its definition explicitly permits this per-copy error. This does not by itself give the same theorem when every output must be correct simultaneously.

context_blocks.title: A new preprint claims progress for global error
context_blocks.text: Suruga’s August 2026 preprint claims an exact asymptotic characterization of expected communication under global error by zero-error internal information complexity, and constant-factor bounds for worst-case amortized communication. It further claims that the strong direct sum fails for relations by combining this characterization with a search-problem separation. These are recorded as preprint claims, without an independent verification of their proofs.

context_blocks.title: The preprint retains a total-function question
context_blocks.text: Immediately after Corollary 1, the preprint states that a corresponding separation for total functions remains open. Thus its claimed relation counterexample cannot justify declaring every randomized direct-sum question resolved. The task-class omission in the original source matters to both formulation and current status.

cards.context:
The source contrasts near-perfect nondeterministic direct sums with failures in a deterministic setting and an open randomized setting. It is a brief motivation for studying composition, not a formal statement of all the conventions needed for this benchmark.

Braverman and Rao’s report characterizes amortized distributional communication by internal information cost when error is bounded separately on each coordinate. Its definition explicitly permits this per-copy error. This does not by itself give the same theorem when every output must be correct simultaneously.

Suruga’s August 2026 preprint claims an exact asymptotic characterization of expected communication under global error by zero-error internal information complexity, and constant-factor bounds for worst-case amortized communication. It further claims that the strong direct sum fails for relations by combining this characterization with a search-problem separation. These are recorded as preprint claims, without an independent verification of their proofs.

Immediately after Corollary 1, the preprint states that a corresponding separation for total functions remains open. Thus its claimed relation counterexample cannot justify declaring every randomized direct-sum question resolved. The task-class omission in the original source matters to both formulation and current status.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
